relationship_to_restored_text: Interpretive contemplative layer aligned by verse. This does not replace the source-audited restored translation.

verses.mystical_translation: Solomon is young, while the assembly is told that his project belongs to Divine rather than human ambition.
Gold, silver, bronze, iron, wood, and stones gather from creation and economy into one sacred plan.
David turns private treasure into a public model of devotion.
The scale of gold and silver overwhelms ordinary imagination.
Artisans await materials while the king asks who will fill the hand willingly.
Those nearest power answer first with gifts.
More immense wealth enters the institutional treasury.
Precious stones move under named financial custody.
Joy is attached to willing generosity, though royal pressure remains possible.
David turns the assembly's attention from donor prestige to YHWH.
Kingdom, power, glory, earth, and heaven are returned in language to Divine ownership.
Wealth and honor are relativized beneath the power to strengthen all.
Thanksgiving answers the name beyond the treasure.
The givers confess that they return what they first received.
The community names itself as migrants and shadows, loosening the grip of possession.
The temple abundance is acknowledged as gift rather than royal self-creation.
Integrity and willingness are celebrated, while only Divine—not leaders—can judge the heart.
David asks that generosity become a lasting inward orientation.
He asks wholeness of heart for the young builder.
The assembly bows toward Divine and king, a dangerous proximity that must not confuse homage with worship.
Three thousand animals die while abundance becomes a national feast.
Eating, drinking, anointing, and joy formalize Solomon's succession.
The throne is called YHWH's, language that cannot make its human occupant Divine.
The archive imagines every leader, warrior, and royal son submitting without conflict.
Solomon receives unprecedented public majesty.
David's reign is summarized over all Israel.
Forty royal years are divided between Hebron and Jerusalem.
David dies with age, wealth, and honor, but a good ending does not cancel those he harmed.
The reign is said to survive in prophetic records beyond Chronicles.
The book closes David's story across king, people, and surrounding kingdoms.

contemplative_note: The final prayer says the people are sojourners and all wealth is borrowed. That confession is the antidote to the chapter's royal abundance. Giving is sacred only when it is free; leadership is sacred only when it is human and accountable; remembrance is sacred only when David's honor does not erase Bathsheba, Uriah, Tamar, the plague dead, conquered peoples, workers, and animals.
